Find the arc length of the line $y=3x+1$ from $x=0$ to $x=4$, and verify your answer using the distance formula.
For $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$, state the condition on $p$ for convergence, and explain why using the antiderivative $\frac{x^{1-p}}{1-p}$ (for $p\neq1$).
questions.answer: Converges when $p>1$. As $b\rightarrow\infty$, $b^{1-p}\rightarrow0$ only when $1-p<0$, i.e. $p>1$; otherwise the limit is infinite (or, for $p=1$, the antiderivative is $\ln x$, which also diverges).
questions.explanation: Converges when $p>1$. As $b\rightarrow\infty$, $b^{1-p}\rightarrow0$ only when $1-p<0$, i.e. $p>1$; otherwise the limit is infinite (or, for $p=1$, the antiderivative is $\ln x$, which also diverges).

questions.q: Evaluate $\int_0^2 \frac{1}{(x-1)^2}\,dx$, or explain why it diverges (note the integrand is undefined at $x=1$, inside the interval).
questions.target: Improper integrals with infinite discontinuities inside the interval
questions.answer: Split at $x=1$: $\int_0^1\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}dx + \int_1^2\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}dx$. Near $x=1$ from either side, $\lim_{b\rightarrow1}\left[-\frac{1}{x-1}\right]$ blows up to $\pm\infty$: both pieces diverge, so the full integral diverges.
questions.explanation: Split at $x=1$: $\int_0^1\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}dx + \int_1^2\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}dx$. Near $x=1$ from either side, $\lim_{b\rightarrow1}\left[-\frac{1}{x-1}\right]$ blows up to $\pm\infty$: both pieces diverge, so the full integral diverges.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{x^{1/3}}\,dx$ (an odd function with a discontinuity at $x=0$), splitting at $x=0$.
questions.target: Improper integrals with infinite discontinuities inside the interval
questions.answer: By symmetry (odd integrand), $\int_{-1}^0 x^{-1/3}dx = -\int_0^1 x^{-1/3}dx$ (each piece converges since $p=\frac{1}{3}<1$ for this type of integrand near a finite discontinuity). The two pieces cancel: the integral equals $0$.
questions.explanation: By symmetry (odd integrand), $\int_{-1}^0 x^{-1/3}dx = -\int_0^1 x^{-1/3}dx$ (each piece converges since $p=\frac{1}{3}<1$ for this type of integrand near a finite discontinuity). The two pieces cancel: the integral equals $0$.

questions.q: The graph shows $f(x)=\frac{1}{x^2}$ on $[1,10]$. As the right boundary extends to infinity, the shaded area approaches a finite limit. Explain why this is plausible, using the fact that $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx=1$ (found earlier).
questions.target: Visualizing an improper integral as a limiting area
questions.answer: The curve $y=\frac{1}{x^2}$ decreases rapidly toward $0$, so the strips added as $x$ grows contribute less and less area. Even though the region extends infinitely far right, the total shaded area converges to a finite value, $1$, because the tail contributions shrink fast enough (consistent with the $p$-test, $p=2>1$).
questions.explanation: The curve $y=\frac{1}{x^2}$ decreases rapidly toward $0$, so the strips added as $x$ grows contribute less and less area. Even though the region extends infinitely far right, the total shaded area converges to a finite value, $1$, because the tail contributions shrink fast enough (consistent with the $p$-test, $p=2>1$).

questions.q: Set up (do not evaluate) the arc length integral for $y=x^2$ on $[0,2]$, and estimate it using the straight-line distance between the endpoints as a lower bound.
questions.target: Arc length of a more involved curve
questions.answer: $y'=2x$: $L=\int_0^2\sqrt{1+4x^2}\,dx$. Straight-line distance between $(0,0)$ and $(2,4)$: $\sqrt{4+16}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5}\approx4.47$, which is a lower bound since the actual curve is longer than the chord connecting its endpoints.
questions.explanation: $y'=2x$: $L=\int_0^2\sqrt{1+4x^2}\,dx$. Straight-line distance between $(0,0)$ and $(2,4)$: $\sqrt{4+16}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5}\approx4.47$, which is a lower bound since the actual curve is longer than the chord connecting its endpoints.

questions.q: Use a comparison with $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$ (known to converge) to argue that $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2+1}\,dx$ also converges, without evaluating it.
questions.answer: For $x\geq1$, $\frac{1}{x^2+1}<\frac{1}{x^2}$. Since $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$ converges (to $1$), and the integrand of interest is smaller and positive everywhere on $[1,\infty)$, the comparison test guarantees $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x^2+1}\,dx$ also converges.
questions.explanation: For $x\geq1$, $\frac{1}{x^2+1}<\frac{1}{x^2}$. Since $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$ converges (to $1$), and the integrand of interest is smaller and positive everywhere on $[1,\infty)$, the comparison test guarantees $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x^2+1}\,dx$ also converges.

questions.q: Use a comparison with $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x}\,dx$ (known to diverge) to argue that $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx$ also diverges.
questions.answer: For $x\geq1$, $\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\geq\frac{1}{x}$ (since $\sqrt{x}\leq x$). Since $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x}\,dx$ diverges and the integrand of interest is even larger, the comparison test guarantees $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx$ also diverges.
questions.explanation: For $x\geq1$, $\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\geq\frac{1}{x}$ (since $\sqrt{x}\leq x$). Since $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x}\,dx$ diverges and the integrand of interest is even larger, the comparison test guarantees $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx$ also diverges.

Level 2 · MediumApply the Ratio Test to determine the convergence or divergence of $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{4^n}{n!}$.
questions.target: Improper integrals with infinite discontinuities inside the interval
questions.answer: Set up the ratio: $\rho = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right| = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left| \frac{4^{n+1}}{(n+1)!} \cdot \frac{n!}{4^n} \right| = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left( \frac{4^{n+1}}{4^n} \cdot \frac{n!}{(n+1)n!} \right) = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{4}{n+1} = 0.$ Since \(\rho = 0 Ratio Test, the series converges absolutely.
questions.explanation: Set up the ratio: $\rho = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right| = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left| \frac{4^{n+1}}{(n+1)!} \cdot \frac{n!}{4^n} \right| = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left( \frac{4^{n+1}}{4^n} \cdot \frac{n!}{(n+1)n!} \right) = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{4}{n+1} = 0.$ Since \(\rho = 0 Ratio Test, the series converges absolutely.

questions.q: Level 1 · FoundationsFind all values of $c$ in the open interval $(-1, 2)$ that satisfy the Mean Value Theorem for $f(x) = x^3 - 2x^2 + 1$.
questions.answer: 1. Check hypotheses: $f(x)$ is a polynomial, continuous on $[-1, 2]$ and differentiable on $(-1, 2)$. 2. Calculate the average rate of change on $[-1, 2]$: $f(-1) = (-1)^3 - 2(-1)^2 + 1 = -1 - 2 + 1 = -2$ $f(2) = 2^3 - 2(2)^2 + 1 = 8 - 8 + 1 = 1$ $\frac{f(2) - f(-1)}{2 - (-1)} = \frac{1 - (-2)}{3} = \frac{3}{3} = 1$ 3. Set $f'(c) = 1$: $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 4x \Rightarrow 3c^2 - 4c = 1 \Rightarrow 3c^2 - 4c - 1 = 0$ Apply the quadratic formula: $c = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{(-4)^2 - 4(3)(-1)}}{2(3)} = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{16 + 12}}{6} = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{28}}{6} = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{7}}{3}$ Evaluating approximations: $\frac{2 + 2.646}{3} \approx 1.549 \in (-1, 2)$ and $\frac{2 - 2.646}{3} \approx -0.215 \in (-1, 2)$. Both values lie strictly inside $(-1, 2)$: $\mathbf{c = \frac{2 - \sqrt{7}}{3}} \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \mathbf{c = \frac{2 + \sqrt{7}}{3}}.$
questions.explanation: 1. Check hypotheses: $f(x)$ is a polynomial, continuous on $[-1, 2]$ and differentiable on $(-1, 2)$. 2. Calculate the average rate of change on $[-1, 2]$: $f(-1) = (-1)^3 - 2(-1)^2 + 1 = -1 - 2 + 1 = -2$ $f(2) = 2^3 - 2(2)^2 + 1 = 8 - 8 + 1 = 1$ $\frac{f(2) - f(-1)}{2 - (-1)} = \frac{1 - (-2)}{3} = \frac{3}{3} = 1$ 3. Set $f'(c) = 1$: $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 4x \Rightarrow 3c^2 - 4c = 1 \Rightarrow 3c^2 - 4c - 1 = 0$ Apply the quadratic formula: $c = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{(-4)^2 - 4(3)(-1)}}{2(3)} = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{16 + 12}}{6} = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{28}}{6} = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{7}}{3}$ Evaluating approximations: $\frac{2 + 2.646}{3} \approx 1.549 \in (-1, 2)$ and $\frac{2 - 2.646}{3} \approx -0.215 \in (-1, 2)$. Both values lie strictly inside $(-1, 2)$: $\mathbf{c = \frac{2 - \sqrt{7}}{3}} \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \mathbf{c = \frac{2 + \sqrt{7}}{3}}.$

questions.q: A random variable $X$ has distribution $\mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$. A single observation of $X$ is taken to test $H_0: \lambda = 6$ against $H_1: \lambda < 6$ at the 5% level. (a) Find the critical region. (b) State the actual significance level. (c) Find the probability of a Type II error if the true value of $\lambda$ is 3.
questions.answer: (a) Under $H_0$, $X \sim \mathrm{Po}(6)$. Calculate cumulative probabilities: $P(X = 0) = e^{-6} \approx 0.00248$ $P(X \leq 1) = e^{-6}(1 + 6) = 7e^{-6} \approx 0.01735$ $P(X \leq 2) = e^{-6}(1 + 6 + 18) = 25e^{-6} \approx 0.06197$ Since $P(X \leq 1) 0.05$, the critical region is $X \leq 1$ (i.e. $X = 0$ or $1$). (b) Actual significance level = $P(X \leq 1 \mid \lambda = 6) = 7e^{-6} \approx 0.0174$ (or 1.74%). (c) Type II error occurs when we fail to reject $H_0$ when $\lambda = 3$. We fail to reject when $X \geq 2$: $P(X \geq 2 \mid \lambda = 3) = 1 - P(X \leq 1 \mid \lambda = 3) = 1 - e^{-3}(1 + 3) = 1 - 4e^{-3} \approx 1 - 0.1991 = 0.801\mathrm{\ (3\ s.f.)}$
questions.explanation: (a) Under $H_0$, $X \sim \mathrm{Po}(6)$. Calculate cumulative probabilities: $P(X = 0) = e^{-6} \approx 0.00248$ $P(X \leq 1) = e^{-6}(1 + 6) = 7e^{-6} \approx 0.01735$ $P(X \leq 2) = e^{-6}(1 + 6 + 18) = 25e^{-6} \approx 0.06197$ Since $P(X \leq 1) 0.05$, the critical region is $X \leq 1$ (i.e. $X = 0$ or $1$). (b) Actual significance level = $P(X \leq 1 \mid \lambda = 6) = 7e^{-6} \approx 0.0174$ (or 1.74%). (c) Type II error occurs when we fail to reject $H_0$ when $\lambda = 3$. We fail to reject when $X \geq 2$: $P(X \geq 2 \mid \lambda = 3) = 1 - P(X \leq 1 \mid \lambda = 3) = 1 - e^{-3}(1 + 3) = 1 - 4e^{-3} \approx 1 - 0.1991 = 0.801\mathrm{\ (3\ s.f.)}$

questions.q: Use $x=u+v, y=u-v$ to compute $\iint_D(x-y)e^{x+y}\,dA$ where $D$ is the square $|x-y|\leq1, |x+y|\leq1$:
questions.target: Arc length of a more involved curve
questions.answer: Under the change of variables $2u = x+y$ and $2v = x-y$, the integrand $2v\,e^{2u}$ is odd in $v$ over the symmetric interval $[-1/2, 1/2]$, so the double integral equals $0$.
